title: torch.einsum 400x slower than numpy.einsum on a simple contraction
body:
## Issue description

`torch.einsum` is 400x slower than `numpy.einsum` on a simple contraction. This is making some Pyro models very slow.

## Code example

```py
import torch, numpy, timeit
x = torch.randn((2, 2000))
y = torch.randn((2, 2, 2000))
equation = 'ac,abc->cb'

time0 = timeit.default_timer()
for _ in range(1000):
    _ = torch.einsum(equation, [x, y])

time1 = timeit.default_timer()
for _ in range(1000):
    _ = numpy.einsum(equation, x.numpy(), y.numpy())

time2 = timeit.default_timer()
print('torch: {}'.format(time1 - time0))
print('numpy: {}'.format(time2 - time1))
```
```
torch: 3.97460007668
numpy: 0.00863790512085
```

```

Quite likely, bmm doesn't like large batches of small multiplications. When replacing "2" by "200" as the smaller dimensions, there is a single digit factor between the speeds (which still is rather large).
If possible, I'd like to fix this in bmm, but I haven't tracked down the root cause yet.

time2 = timeit.default_timer()

for _ in range(1000):
    _ = torch.bmm(xp, yp)
time3 = timeit.default_timer()

# check that we calculate the right thing.
print((torch.einsum(equation, [x, y])-torch.bmm(xp, yp).squeeze()).abs().max().item())

print('torch: {}'.format(time1 - time0))
print('numpy: {}'.format(time2 - time1))
print('torch.bmm: {}'.format(time3 - time2))
```

[t-vi | 2018-08-29T07:42:19Z]
So the inefficiency comes from `bmm` on CPU iterating over the batch dimension and relegating to the matrix multiplication.
I have a tentative CPU fix that just spells out the bmm contraction (currently for `batch > 10 * contraction size`, but I would need to investigate the tradeoff) and parallelizes over the batch dimension.

The GPU bmm uses cublas' batch gemm (if available / applicable) so I would leave that alone for the moment unless we identify inferior performance there, too. I don't know how it compares e.g. to magma.

Fun facts:
- Numpy's `bmm` actually delegates to numpy's einsum which has all sorts of contraction operations for various setups.
- MKL seems to have a batch gemm, one might use that eventually.

title: `profiler.table()` too slow
body:
## Issue description

When processing large amount of output lines(about 100000 lines), profiler.table() can spend several minutes. I think it's because in `build_table()`, new lines are added to the end of a string, and this can result in a copy operation of the whole string. The best practise here may be using `StringIO`.

title: torch.multinomial performance issue when replacement=False
body:
## Issue description

`torch.multinomial` becomes very slow if the `replacement=False` and the `num_samples` is relatively large.

## Code example
```
import torch
weights = torch.randn(10000000, dtype=torch.float32).clamp(0.01, 1)

n_small = 100
n_big = 100000

# Works
sample_1 = torch.multinomial(weights, n_small, replacement=True)
print("Sampled 1")

# Works
sample_2 = torch.multinomial(weights, n_big, replacement=True)
print("Sampled 2")

# Works, but much slower
sample_3 = torch.multinomial(weights, n_small, replacement=False)
print("Sampled 3")

# I think it works, but it takes so long that it is unusable
sample_4 = torch.multinomial(weights, n_big, replacement=False)

[t-vi | 2018-09-21T10:16:10Z]
This is expected as the non-repeating actually makes sampling a serial process. While there is room for optimization relative to the current way of doing things, I don't think you can this to get much better when you have many samples.

[bfreskura | 2018-09-21T10:56:25Z]
Numpy function `choice` works normally for large inputs and large samples:
`x = np.random.choice(1000000, 100000, replace=False)`

Isn't this the same as `torch.multinomial`?

---

[t-vi | 2018-09-21T11:16:54Z]
Not quite, it's more like
`a = numpy.random.choice(1_000_000, 100_000, replace=False, p=probs)`
but you're absolutely right, we are unreasonably slow there.
Thank you for reporting and insisting!

---

[t-vi | 2018-09-21T11:35:55Z]
So what numpy does is approximately (it's easy for the non-batched case):
```
p = torch.ones(1_000_000)
have = 0
want = 100_000
p_ = p.clone()
result = torch.empty(want, dtype=torch.long)
while have < want:
    a = torch.multinomial(p_, want-have, replacement=True)
    b = a.unique()
    result[have:have+b.size(-1)] = b
    p_[b] = 0
    have += b.size(-1)
```
so it will attempt (but fail) to get all samples, but will be much more efficient than sampling only one at a time and renormalizing the pdf after each sample.
I'll implement this, but I can't promise to get it done before 1.0.

title: BN gets dramatically slow when batch_size exceeds a threshold
body:
## Issue description
I use ```torch.nn.BatchNorm1d``` in my code. When the batchsize of the input exceeds a threshold, BN gets very slow. This problem can be produced on my machine with the code (test_bn.py) provided below.

For example, in the following output I test it with input of size (5x20000, 256), (6x20000, 256), (7x20000, 256) and (8x20000, 256). The magnitude of the running time changes after 6.

```bash
~$ CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=5 python test_bn.py 5

backward: 0.019s
total: 0.026s
~$ CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=5 python test_bn.py 6
forward: 0.007s
backward: 0.022s
total: 0.030s
~$ CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=5 python test_bn.py 7
forward: 0.135s
backward: 0.102s
total: 0.237s
~$ CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=5 python test_bn.py 8
forward: 0.155s
backward: 0.117s
total: 0.271s
```

## Code example
```python
# test_bn.py
import torch
import time
import sys

bs = int(sys.argv[1])
num_features = 256

shape = torch.Size((bs * 20000, num_features))
input = torch.cuda.FloatTensor(shape)
torch.randn(shape, out=input)
input.requires_grad = True

bn = torch.nn.BatchNorm1d(num_features, eps=1e-05, momentum=0.1, affine=True, track_running_stats=True)
bn.cuda()

N = 30
forward_time = 0
backward_time = 0
for i in range(N):
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    start = time.time()
    output = bn(input)
    output = output.mean()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    forward_time += time.time() - start

    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    start = time.time()
    output.backward()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    backward_time += time.time() - start

print('forward: %f', forward_time / N)
print('backward: %f', backward_time / N)
print('total: %f', (forward_time + backward_time) / N)
```

In this case, the shape of the input is ```NxC```. If ```N>131070```, cuDNN can't handle it and it will be processed by THCUNN.

According to the following code in THCUNN, it will be inefficient because ```input.getSize(0) = N, input.getSize(2) = 1``` and ```N``` is large. So __2d input to ```torch.nn.BatchNorm1d``` will cause low utilization of GPU__. To solve this problem, we can transpose and reshape the input to ```1xCxN```. According to my test, cuDNN has the same problem.
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/8ff435c8f60033d6f7795202d145e738a551ee84/aten/src/THCUNN/BatchNormalization.cu#L171-L176

title: Potential memory leak in Tensor.size()
body:
## 🐛 Bug

Tensor.size() leaks 28 bytes of memory (similar to the previously resolved issue of #1963)

## To Reproduce

```
import torch, tracemalloc; tracemalloc.start()

def main():
    def loop(maximum):
        tmp = torch.Tensor(maximum)
        for _ in range(1000):
            sizes = tmp.size()
    snapshot1 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
    loop(maximum=256)
    snapshot2 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
    loop(maximum=257)
    snapshot3 = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
    for line in snapshot2.compare_to(snapshot1, 'lineno')[:10]:
        print(line)
    print()
    for line in snapshot3.compare_to(snapshot2, 'lineno')[:10]:
        print(line)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Expected behavior

This will give you something similar to the line below only in the second run, but this should not happen.
```

title: LSTM memory leak?
body:
The following script consumes about 1 GB of memory in 100 iterations, and continually increases memory usage. It's a stripped down version of a larger file to isolate the potential leak.

Commenting out lines 33-34 stabilizes memory usage to 30 MB.

```python
import numpy as np
import torch

from torch.autograd import Variable

class PolicyNet(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, layers):
        super(PolicyNet, self).__init__()
        self.lstm = torch.nn.LSTMCell(layers[0], layers[1])
        self.linear = torch.nn.Linear(layers[1], layers[2])
        self.layers = layers

    def forward(self, x, h0, c0):
        h1, c1 = self.lstm(x, (h0, c0))
        o1 = self.linear(h1)
        return o1, h1, c1

def leak(policy_net):
    # Prepare for one forward pass, with the batch containing the entire episode
    h_n_batch = Variable(torch.zeros(1000, 32))
    c_n_batch = Variable(torch.zeros(1000, 32))
    softmax = torch.nn.Softmax()

    # Batch input to LSTM has size [num_agents, episode_len, lstm_input_size]
    input_batch = Variable(torch.zeros(2, 1000, 5))

    # Do a forward pass, and fill sum_log_probs with sum(log(p)) for each time-step
    sum_log_probs = Variable(torch.zeros(1000))
    for i in range(2):
        o_n, h_n_batch, c_n_batch = policy_net(input_batch[i], h_n_batch, c_n_batch)
        dist = softmax(o_n)
        ### Comment out L33-34 to stop memory leak ###
        for j in range(1000):
            sum_log_probs[j] = sum_log_probs[j] + torch.log(dist[j, 0])

if __name__ == '__main__':
    policy_net = PolicyNet([5, 32, 3])

    for i in range(10000):
        leak(policy_net)
        print(i)
```

This is for version `0.1.12_2` on macOS 10.12.4.

title: [RFC] Integration with MKL-DNN
body:
## 🚀 Feature
Two options:
- Opaque integration akin to the current Caffe2’s ideep tensor. The tensor would support only a subset of operations that are explicitly implemented and fine-grained access of the tensor will not be efficient (e.g. operator[]). This is how e.g. sparse tensors are supported today. Note, that TensorImpl doesn’t need to be virtualized for it as top-level tensor operations (including resize_ and all math/nn ops) go through the dispatch mechanism (in TensorMethods.h and a few other places) and can be routed to another implementation.
- Fine grained integration where PyTorch has visibility into what MKLDNN layout is. In this case majority of tensor ops would work and even many regular PT kernels would work against mkldnn tensors if they rely on TensorAccessor and friends. It’s a more powerful integration and provides a better UX but it’d require “opening the covers” for MKLDNN and also higher complexity for core PT code to recognize other layouts.
comments:
[ezyang | 2019-01-15T17:59:48Z]
cc @colesbury

---

[ezyang | 2019-01-15T18:02:09Z]
Another way of stating the pitch for option (2), is a recognition of the fact that a tensor X represented in blocked format, is still a tensor X. So if you say X + Y, where one is blocked, and the other is not, you'd expect this to still give you a result (even if it's slow to compute.) Just like how we call X.contiguous() when X is strided and we have a kernel that doesn't understand strides.

---

[colesbury | 2019-01-15T21:19:28Z]
Some minor points:
- This doesn't have much to do with TensorImpl being virtual or not. You can support blocked layouts and still have TensorImpl be non-virtual.
- The MKL-DNN layout is documented in [Understanding Memory Formats](https://intel.github.io/mkl-dnn/understanding_memory_formats.html).
- It's probably *not* worth supporting blocked layouts in TensorAccessor. TensorAccessor isn't very efficient to start-with and the extra modulo (%) operation will likely slow it down. It's probably worth it to support it in something like TensorIterator, at least for element-wise kernels, since we can re-arrange and combine dimensions to avoid expensive indexing.
- A fine grained integration will require a lot of work. Even the minimum of throwing an error for unsupported layouts will require substantial work. (And it would be better to do something like @ezyang's comment about X.contiguous())

---

[Jianhui-Li | 2019-02-14T17:46:31Z]
We had a couple of internal discussions on this and converged that we probably can't afford the second option which allows broad set of Pytorch ops to access MKL-DNN block format directly. There are multiple blocking format for activation depending on the data type, and are many for weight. Given the feedback above on the efforts and complexity concerns raised in the PR, we also think it is better to take the first option where the MKL-DNN tensors supports a subset of ops which are most frequent executed and performance critical. 

One thing needs to be aware of is that MKL-DNN blocking format cannot be decided at the static time. The data format is decided at run time by MKL-DNN algorithm depending on the input tensor shape and data type. So the reordering has to be done at run time. The reordering may be needed between a serious of MKL-DNN convolution ops (like between group conv and regular conv for certain shape). The MKL-DNN integration layer needs to check the incoming tensor's format, query the expected format from MKL-DNN, and does the reordering on the fly.

One of our design goal is to reduce layout reordering. Instead of converting the MKL-DNN block format back to plain format at the end of each operation, we would like to have lazy reordering so that the activation tensor can stay in MKL-DNN format when it travels through MKL-DNN operations. When the activation tensor leaves the MKL-DNN op, it could stay in blocking format without reordering, and upon dispatch time, the tensor is converted to the format expected by the next op.

---

[ezyang | 2019-02-14T22:43:52Z]
Thanks. We'll have to move forward with this as an opaque integration then

---

[Jianhui-Li | 2019-02-22T07:58:35Z]
We (Intel Pytorch team) have a couple of discussions with @bddppq on whether MKL-DNN op should be visible to user and how MKL-DNN op should be implemented in Pytorch C10 backend.  We summarize the discussion below to capture the motivation and directions on the high level design.  Your feedback is welcome.

====
The Pytorch C10 design would like to make MKL-DNN operation visible to user. So if user wants to use MKL-DNN operations, user needs to explicitly convert cpu tensor to MKL-DNN tensor, and vice versa.  The motivation of explicit user conversion is to support performance debugging. If the conversion is done implicitly in the C10 ops/runtime, the model designer may produce a model with hidden conversion cost which it is hard to debug the conversion related performance issues during the deploy time. When the pytorch program is statically compiled to a computation graph, C10 would like to able to differentiate MKL-DNN op from cpu op in the computation graph, and the tensor conversion is represented as a node in the graph. This facilitates the graph optimization and also ease the performance debugging. This involves changes in both Pytorch front-end and back-end. Pytorch front-end needs to expose MKL-DNN to user through certain mechanism, and Pytorch back-end needs to treat MKL-DNN as a backend device so the MKL-DNN OP is represented as Aten OP’s implementation on MKL-DNN device.
 
Intel Pytroch team would like to have the MKL-DNN optimization enabled without user changing code. With the computation graph, an optimization pass may be done to promote CPU op to MKL-DNN op, and add or delete the format conversion op for best performance. The optimization pass ensures that the graph path can enjoy the performance benefit from the latest MKL-DNN version without user changing the program.
 
FB Pytorch team understands that MKL-DNN op decides the input/output tensor format at runtime. The user specified to_mkl-dnn() may not trigger the actual format conversion, which may actually happen at the entry of the following MKL-DNN op. The user specified to_cpu() usually triggers a conversion since the MKL-DNN tensor is typically not the plain format. The format conversion may happen between two consecutive MKL-DNN ops.
 
Intel Pytorch team would like to not confuse Pytroch user taking MKL-DNN as a HW device. As MKL-DNN is essentially an optimization library on the base device (CPU), calling  MKL-DNN a device on Pytorch front-end may cause confusion. For example, the MKL-DNN library may extended to cover another Intel device in the future, in that case, user may be confused by a MKL-DNN device on top of the new Intel device. So, if the MKL-DNN OP has to be exposed in Pytorch front-end, it may be exposed as OPs working with special format tensors, not a device.  It is like how sparse tensor is presented to user using torch.to_sparse(), so it could be tensor.to_mkl-dnn(), not tensor.to(device='mkl-dnn-x86').
 
In early experiment stage, if Pytorch user (model designer) complains such usage model, Pytorch team may consider a Python compatible layer, which enlarges MKL-DNN operation scope by simply implementing the non-MKL-DNN Ops by a conversion to cpu tensor and cpu op implementation.  This simplifies MKL-DNN op usage since user only needs to specify the conversion to MKL-DNN format at the beginning of the program, but it also defeat the purpose of having user aware of the conversion and an accurate computation graph.

---

[uyongw | 2019-03-27T08:34:02Z]
@yinghai @ezyang As for the 2nd choice, I know currently PyTorch does not even support NHWC plain format. If we uncover MKL-DNN blocked format in the tensor integration, will it break the design philosophy indicated from https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/1220 ?

---

[Jianhui-Li | 2019-04-05T07:17:03Z]
Beside activation, MKL-DNN weight also requires blocking format so we need to reorder the weight before feeding to the MKL-DNN primitives. There are two options: user needs to reorder the weight for MKL-DNN op, or user don't need. Following discussions with some Pytorch developers, we are heading the direction that user don’t need to reorder the weight in the program. In the JIT path, the weight are reordered at the graph init time. In the impreative path, the MKL-DNN OP accept CPU weight tensor with public format.  We would like to post this direction here to get feedback from stakeholders and community. @yinghai @ezyang @dzhulgakov @Soumith @gchanan @bddppq @mingfeima @uyongw @jiong5

---

[dzhulgakov | 2019-04-05T07:28:23Z]
I think it's a good idea to do weights prepacking, but it should be opt-in (as e.g. some ops for a custom optimizer might not be implemented on mkldnn tensor). Effectively, we just need to walk parameters of a module in question and change them to mkldnn - we can expose it on module as `mod.mkldnn()` similarly to `mod.cuda()`.

The tricky part would be behavior during serialization - it's unclear whether after save/load cycle the tensor should stay as mkldnn.

---

[Jianhui-Li | 2019-04-05T17:11:31Z]
Thanks @dzhulgakov for the feedback.

For user opt-in approach, there is an issue that mod.mkldnn() reorders weights for all the MKL-DNN op in the model but activation tensor.to_mkldnn()/to_dense() may specify a smaller scope of MKL-DNN ops due to the program was developer at an ealrier Pytorch with less MKL-DNN op support.  In the JIT path,  we assume that we could expand the activation scope to match with weight.  However, in the imperative path, the out of scope activation tensor (in CPU dense format) is dispatched to CPU device not MKL-DNN device, but with the weight reordered for MKL-DNN.  There are multiple options to solve this - 1) change CPU OP to accept MKL-DNN format tensor; 2) change the dispatch to send the pair (activation in CPU, weight in MKL-DNN) to MKL-DNN op which needs to be enhanced to input CPU activation other than MKL-DNN activation, 3) leave the issue as is, user should expect the issue for Pytorch upgrade.   All looks unnatural to me.

This issue above is the main reason why we think we may not want to follow CUDA style for explicit weight transfer - which is a must to run op on a separate device so user may accept option 3) above.  But MKL-DNN is fundamentally not a device,  and it only accelerates small amount of operations. The reordering cost is much smaller than dispatching to a device.  The purpose of having user aware of using MKL-DNN is already fulfilled by requiring tensor.to_mkldnn()/to_dense().

---

[jgong5 | 2019-04-06T00:44:55Z]
@dzhulgakov Consider the custom optimizer case you mentioned, and users *don't* need to change the weight format, we guarantee that MKL-DNN backward op always returns the same tensor type as weight for gradient, i.e. weight/gradient in CPU tensor (imperative path) or weight/gradient in MKL-DNN tensor (JIT path). Is that OK?

> The tricky part would be behavior during serialization - it's unclear whether after save/load cycle the tensor should stay as mkldnn.

I think they should be serialized as CPU tensors to be compatible in most cases.

---

implemented in some form now.

title: multivariate_normal.log_prob is slow
body:
## 🐛 Bug

On the discussion forums, user Al3x reported a severe performance regression - from subsecond to almost 9 minutes:
https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/going-from-0-4-0-to-1-0-0-changes-code-runtime-from-000-35-to-045-63/37200/15
The problematic bit is MultivariateNormal. I tracked this down to `_batch_mahalanobis` and it's use  of `_batch_trtrs_lower`. In 0.4 it used (a list comprehension over non-batched, because we didn't have it) torch.inverse instead of `trtrs`.

## To Reproduce

```
mu = torch.randn(8)
sigma = torch.eye(8).expand(6, 1, 8, 8).contiguous().requires_grad_()
x_repeat = torch.randn(6,8000,8)
pdf = MultivariateNormal(mu, sigma).log_prob(x_repeat).t()
pdf.sum().backward()
```

More specific code is also in the forum thread.

## Expected behavior

The old speed!

## Environment

Masterish PyTorch and comparison to 0.4.1.

## Additional context

I'm undecided whether it's `_batch_mahalanobis`' or `trtrs`'s fault. Probably we should have a triangular solver primitive without the funny extra copy return and a batch version, too.

CC some distribution gurus @fehiepsi and @fritzo and batch-linear-algebra hero @vishwakftw
comments:
[fehiepsi | 2019-02-16T22:44:42Z]
@t-vi Thanks for notifying me! I think that it is my fault when trying to use `trtrs` instead of `inverse`. The slowdown seems lie at [this line](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/distributions/multivariate_normal.py#L43) where we expand `bL` batch shape to match the later part of `bx` batch shape, then do triangle solve with "expanded" bL. If we use `inverse`, then after taking the inverse of `bL`, we just simply do `matmul` with `bx` to get the result. So it will be much faster in the above example.

The current implementation works well when `x` has additional batch shapes instead. For example, the following version will be fast because we won't expand bL.
```
sigma = torch.eye(8).expand(6, 1, 8, 8).contiguous().requires_grad_()
x_repeat = torch.randn(8000, 6, 1, 8)
```

I'll sketch out a solution which I have in mind for further discussion.

---

[fehiepsi | 2019-02-17T03:31:28Z]
I make a [gist](https://gist.github.com/fehiepsi/da4f45ad00d450ee74ffe6e7809c368a) to show my proposed solution. We can see a huge speed up with @t-vi 's example.

Basically, assume `bL.shape = (i, j, n, n)` and `bx.shape = (K, I, J, n)`, we first reshape `bx` such that
`bx.shape = (K, I / i, i, J / j, j, n)`. Then we move "to-be-expaned" dims to the left by permuting such that
`bx.shape = (K, I / i, J / j, i, j, n)`. Now, we don't need to expand `bL` because the batch_shape (i, j) is matched. After using triangle_solve and getting a result with shape `(K, I / i, J / j, i, j)`, we permute the result to make it have shape `(K, I / i, i, J / j, j)`. A final reshape operator will give shape `(K, I, J)` for the result.

Though this solves the topic's issue, there might be a better solution without having to manipulate reshape+permute operators like this. I'm looking forward to see others' opinions.

Another thing we need to concern is using inverse will be faster for mvn with event_shape <=8 (as shown in the above gist). But trtrs will outperform inverse for larger event_shape.

---

[t-vi | 2019-02-17T11:04:31Z]
Thank you. Your analysis is spot on. That, on the other hand, means that it's not using that using `trtrs` itself is a problem.

In terms of solution, I'd think that getting a good, batch-capable triangular_solve in ATen would be ideal.
For the proper broadcasting:
- trtrs takes c right hand sides in `(n,c)` shape (ugh).
- Prepend singleton dimensions to `bx` until `bx.dim()+1 >= bL.dim()`.
- Move the first `bx.dim() + 1 - bL.dim() ` dimensions of `bx` to the end (after `n`).
- Eliminate any singleton/stride 0 dimensions from `bL` while moving the corresponding dims in`bx` to the right.
- Then each `(n,n)` block in `bL` would correspond to `(n, ...)` bx and one could apply `trtrs` to solve that.
- Finally we need to clean up all the permutation mess. :)

---

[fehiepsi | 2019-02-19T01:44:42Z]
@t-vi Thanks! I forgot that PyTorch only supports broadcasting for `j=1` or `j=J`, so we don't have to `reshape`. :)

Let's wait for others' opinions, then I'll make a PR to fix this issue.

---

[soumith | 2019-02-19T12:13:29Z]
@fehiepsi go for it, it looks like no one else is jumping in with comments.

title: Tensor unfold backward is slow
body:
## 🐛 Bug

Given the following code, the forward pass is very fast but the backward pass is unreasonably slow. I had a look at the backward pass code and while I am not an expert, I think it could be made significantly faster by writing a custom kernel instead of allocating index arrays, especially since `index_add_` seems to be so slow.

title: NCCL uses old(?) CUDA ARCH, causing very slow startup
body:
## 🐛 Bug

On my computer (with GTX1080Ti, CUDA 10) and with today's master, I'm getting extremely slow (60 sec?) startup times. `sudo perf top` (thanks, @soumith) indicates that this is due ptx-jitting. Using NCCL seems to produce sm_30 assembly in the libcaffe2_gpu.so, which I don't get when not using NCCL.

Setting TORCH_CUDA_ARCH=6.1 doesn't help.

## To Reproduce

Compile from source on GTX1080Ti with CUDA 10. With USE_NCCL=1 vs with USE_NCCL=0.
Then initialize any cuda tensor.

title: Inconsistent recovery from CUDA OOMs
body:
## 🐛 Bug

**Editorial note:** Make sure that you are not holding on to tensors via an exception object (which contains the stack trace and will retain tensors). Do not bring the exception object into scope, or do error recovery outside of the catch block.

Catching a RuntimeError on a CUDA OOM should allow one to gracefully recover, for example by lowering the batchsize. This is particularly important when using DistributedDataParallel, where workers must sync on backward, and so it's important that we be able to perform a "dummy batch" after an OOM in order to stay in sync with other workers.

Observed behavior during a CUDA out of memory event is inconsistent across nondistributed/dataparallel/distributeddataparallel. Expected behavior is that all modes should be able to recover easily.

    )

    )

    td.init_process_group(
        backend='nccl',

        world_size=1
    )
    model = tp.DistributedDataParallel(

        device_ids=[0],

    )
    return model


def create_model(args):
    model = nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(INPUT_SIZE, HID_SIZE),
        nn.ReLU(),
    )
    for i in range(LAYERS):
        model.add_module('hidd' + str(i), nn.Linear(HID_SIZE, HID_SIZE))
        model.add_module('relu' + str(i), nn.ReLU())
    model.add_module('output', nn.Linear(HID_SIZE, OUT_CLASSES))
    return model


def fwbw(model, bs):
    print('  Forward with bs  = {:-6d}'.format(bs))
    X = torch.randn(bs, INPUT_SIZE).cuda()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    yhat = model(X)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    loss = yhat.sum()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print('  Backward with bs = {:-6d}'.format(bs))
    loss.backward()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    model.zero_grad()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

    print('Conda PREFIX:', os.environ['CONDA_PREFIX'])

    elif args.mode == 'ddp_multi':

        model = wrap_ddp_multi(model)
    elif args.mode == 'ddp_single':

        torch.cuda.set_device(0)

title: matmul uses too much memory in some batched cases
body:
## 🐛 Bug

PyTorch `1.1.0a0+c3e3c5c`. The GPU times reported are on a P100.

In this case matmul uses about 12 GB of memory when it shouldn't use more than ~3 MB. (i.e. it's using 4096x more memory than necessary)

#### A
```python
x = torch.randn(4096, 4096)
y = torch.randn(192, 4096, 1)
z = torch.matmul(x, y)
```

Note that this is equivalent to the following memory efficient operation:


#### B
```
x = torch.randn(4096, 4096)
y = torch.randn(192, 4096, 1)
z = torch.bmm(x.unsqueeze(0).expand(192, *x.shape), y)
```

It's also equivalent to the following which is memory efficient and faster, but may require a copy of y and the output may be batched-column-major without some extra work:

#### C
```
x = torch.randn(4096, 4096)
y = torch.randn(192, 4096, 1)
z = torch.matmul(y.permute(0, 2, 1), x.t()).permute(0, 2, 1)
```

On GPU, **A** takes ~125 ms and uses 12 GB of memory, **B** takes ~22 ms, and **C** takes ~1 ms.

Originally https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/unexpected-huge-memory-cost-of-matmul/41642/4

See also https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/13222 which may be related

----

I believe the problem is the unnecessary contiguous call here:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/15b318de840de61e2e789c013e34d23819715090/aten/src/ATen/native/LinearAlgebra.cpp#L460-L461

Instead of using `contiguous()` and `view()` it may be possible to use `reshape()`. That might achieve performance of **B**.

title: Potential Memory Leak in expand_as
body:
I think I encountered a memory leak situation potentially due to `expand_as`. I create a [gist](https://gist.github.com/zihangdai/5d4b6fa96ce1366f5bc7268fee0d4e9f) to reproduce my observations.

Basically, for three different (meaningless) models, once the `expand_as` function is used, the memory usage will keep increasing.

To run the code, `python mem_leak_expand.py --run_expand --model_type [0,1,2]` where the `--run_expand` flag controls whether `expand_as` is used. Please run it long enough.

I'm on Ubuntu 14.04 with python3.6. I tried two versions of pytorch, 0.1.12_2 and 0.1.12+da0fad8.

**Side Note**: Even without using `expand_as`, the memory usauge can also increase for a while, but it will finally stablize at a level. What's more, when `Conv2d` (i.e. `--model_type [1,2]`) is used, it can take very long before the memory usage stablizes. I'm not sure whether this is a problem or not.
comments:
[zihangdai | 2017-07-02T22:49:44Z]
I think I'm sure there is a memory leak due to `expand_as`, and I found a weird way to do a temporary fix under pytorch version "0.1.12_2".

The simplest example is as follows:

```python
from __future__ import print_function, division
import gc
import argparse
import resource

import torch
from torch.autograd import Variable

def main(args):
    tgt_var = Variable(torch.rand(32, 512))

    for i in range(args.num_steps):
        src_var = Variable(torch.rand(1, 512))
        if args.fix:
            expanded = src_var.expand(*list(tgt_var.size()))
        else:
            expanded = src_var.expand_as(tgt_var)

        if args.backward:
            ret.mean().backward()

        gc.collect()
        if i > 0 and i % 500 == 0:
            max_mem_used = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
            print("#{} {:.4f} MB".format(i, max_mem_used / 1024))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='PyTorch expand_as memory leak')
    parser.add_argument('--num_steps', type=int, default=1000000)
    parser.add_argument('--backward', action='store_true', default=False)
    parser.add_argument('--fix', action='store_true', default=False)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    main(args)
```

Basically, if we replace `expand_as` with `expand`, and pass in an unpacked list of numbers, (i.e., `src_var.expand(*list(tgt_var.size()))` instead of `src_var.expand(tgt_var.size())`), the memory leak is gone. Using `src_var.expand(tgt_var.size())` will also have the leak issue. Unfortunately, I don't know why this is working.

Finally, since there are so many `expand_as` in pytorch code, to do a quick hacky fix, one can change the `expand_as` function in the file `torch/autograd/variable.py` as follows:
```python
    def expand_as(self, tensor):
        return Expand(list(tensor.size()))(self)
        # return Expand(tensor.size())(self)
```

---

[zihangdai | 2017-07-03T06:00:48Z]
After some more research, I think we have a much bigger problem here. My current conjecture is that: whenever we use `tensor.size()` (`torch.Size` object) as an argument to a function, there will be a memory leak.

An example is the `pad_packed_sequence` function in `torch/nn/utils/rnn.py`, where [line 107](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/nn/utils/rnn.py#L107) of the code is `output = var_data.data.new(len(batch_sizes), max_batch_size, *var_data.size()[1:]).zero_()` which uses `*var_data.size()`.

Again, a minimal example for reproduction is as follows:

```python
from __future__ import print_function, division
import gc
import argparse
import resource

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.autograd import Variable

import torch.nn.utils.rnn as rnn_utils

def main(args):
    max_len = 8
    hid_dim = 16
    batch_s = 4
    model = nn.GRU(hid_dim, hid_dim)
    for i in range(args.num_steps):

        embedding = Variable(torch.rand(max_len, batch_s, hid_dim))
        lengths = range(max_len, max_len-batch_s, -1)

        packed_emb = rnn_utils.pack_padded_sequence(embedding, lengths)
        packed_out, hidden_final = model(packed_emb)
        outputs, srclens = rnn_utils.pad_packed_sequence(packed_out)

        if args.backward:
            outputs.mean().backward()

        gc.collect()
        if i > 0 and i % 500 == 0:
            max_mem_used = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
            print("#{} {:.4f} MB".format(i, max_mem_used / 1024))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='PyTorch *tensor.size() memory leak')
    parser.add_argument('--num_steps', type=int, default=1000000)
    parser.add_argument('--backward', action='store_true', default=False)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    main(args)
```

As in the `expand_as` case, once I change the code to `output = var_data.data.new(len(batch_sizes), max_batch_size, *list(var_data.size())[1:]).zero_()`, memory leak is gone.

So, in short, the problem is on the usage of `tensor.size()`.

title: Performance Regression of Dataloader
body:
## 🐛 Bug

Latest change to Dataloader (#19228) leads to severe performance regression for large scale training up to 30%. We finally root the cause to theses change: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/utils/data/dataloader.py#L889-L891. It causes the exit of each epoch has additional 5 seconds.

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

title: ATen ParallelOpenMP thread_num decision questions
body:
We have noticed some differences in calculating the num_threads to spawn in different ATen Parallel backends, which, as far as we have observed, may lead to degraded performance of OpenMP backend under some circumstances.

In the OpenMP version:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e327df396564f937d17b5f28e2529229260c65bf/aten/src/ATen/ParallelOpenMP.h#L28
The logic seems to be: either do not parallel at all (if num < grain_size), or spawn as many as omp_get_max_threads() threads.

In other backends, e.g. Native:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e327df396564f937d17b5f28e2529229260c65bf/aten/src/ATen/ParallelNative.h#L41-L44
The logic is likely something as: min(get_num_threads(), num / grain_size).

We noticed this problem because after upgrading our PyTorch (>= 1.1.0 in our experince), the DataLoader, with pin_memory=True, is saturating our 36C/72T cpus even with some very small datasets (CIFAR10, resize=32, batch_size=40) and with num_threads=1, however, with no significant training speed boost. Further investigation shows that the copy operation to the pinned memory behaves very differently between two releases. After looking at the code we conjecture that this is due to the overhead that OMP tries to spawn an unecessarily large number of threads for small CPU Tensors.

We installed both PyTorch from conda so we are not absolutely certain about the build options. However we provide some code snippets that may possibly reveal the aformentioned problem:

1. Simple comparisons on copy operation:

``` python

import torch

N = int(argv[1])

a, b = [torch.randn([N]) for _ in (0, 1)]

  b.copy_(a)
```

title: Memory leak in `torch.tensor`
body:
## 🐛 Bug

Calling `torch.tensor` on a Python `list` of `np.float32` objects leaks memory.

## To Reproduce

```
import numpy as np
import torch

def mem():
	import os, psutil
	return psutil.Process(os.getpid()).memory_info().rss // 1024

a = np.zeros(10000, dtype = np.float32) # <-- 1. dtype is important
a = list(a) # <-- 2. has to be a python list

mem_base = mem()
for _ in range(10):
	torch.tensor(a) # <-- 3. must not pass `dtype=torch.float32` here
	print(mem() - mem_base)

# output on my machine:
# 1416
# 2884
# 3940
# 4996
# 6316
# 7372
# 8428
# 9484
# 10804
# 11860
```

## Expected behavior

The number being printed (memory usage) should be more or less constant.

## Environment

 - PyTorch Version: 1.0.0, 1.1.0, 1.2.0
 - OS (e.g., Linux): Linux
 - How you installed PyTorch (`conda`, `pip`, source): pip
 - Python version: 3.6.8

## Additional context

On pytorch==0.4.1, `torch.tensor(a)` throws:
```
RuntimeError: Could not infer dtype of numpy.float32
```

Also, this might be the underlying bug in [#17499](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/17499).

### How this shows up in real code

This shows up in real code if you have a 1d array in a dataset:

```
class Dataset:
    def __init__(self, X, y):
        self.X = x; self.y = y

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self.X[i], self.y[i] # <-- self.y[i] is a np.float32

    def __len__(self):
        return self.X.shape[0]
```

`self.y[i]` is a `np.float32`, and in 1.2.0, a batch of these get wrapped in a `list` by `_MapDatasetFetcher`, and `default_collate` calls `torch.as_tensor` on it.

title: Very high CPU utilization with pin_memory=True and num_workers > 0
body:
## 🐛 Bug
There seems to be an issue with CPU utilization when using a DataLoader with pin_memory=True and num_workers > 0.

I revisited some old code that had `pin_memory=True` and two workers that weren't doing all that much. It pinned all of my CPU cores at or near 100%, with 40-50% of the usage in the kernel.  I've had performance issues with pinned memory in the past, but never to this level. Indeed, I cannot reproduce the issue going back to some older environments with 0.4 or 1.0.1. But on 3 machines w/ PyTorch 1.1 and 1.2 I can easily reproduce by running the MNIST main.py from the current examples master.

If I set either num_workers=0 or pin_memory=False the issue goes away and I'm left with the expected one core and change of usage for MNIST (or two cores and change for my original case).

## To Reproduce

1. Run `main.py` from the MNIST example on master pytorch/examples repository.

## Expected behavior

For MNIST, with 1 worker I expect roughly 1 core's worth of CPU utilization plus some overhead. It consumes 50-100% of all cores on systems with 8-14 physical (16-28 logical) cores. A large % of the CPU usage is in the kernel, appears to be spinning/yielding, possibly due to contention.

## Environment

I've reproduced on 3 machines.

 - PyTorch Version (e.g., 1.0): 1.1 and 1.2 (no issue on an older 1.0.1 and 0.4.1 environment on one of the machines)
 - OS (e.g., Linux): two Ubuntu 18.04 machines, one Ubuntu 16.04 machine
 - How you installed PyTorch (`conda`, `pip`, source): All conda installs
 - Python version: 3.7.3 and 3.6.8
 - CUDA/cuDNN version: Cuda 10 and CUDNN 7.5.1 and 7.6.2
 - GPU models and configuration: dual Titan RTX one one machine, dual Titan Xp and 1080Ti on other two
 - Any other relevant information:

## Additional context
I've seen at least one very likely, and other potential threads in discussion forum that are likely this issue.

This one has an htop screenshot from me, and another user:
https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/cpu-usage-extremely-high/52172/5

title: `at::parallel_for` does not propagate thread-local variables to child threads in embedding_renorm_
body:
See repro below:

```python
import torch

def run(val):
    print("Running :", val)
    weights = torch.rand(100, 64, requires_grad=True)
    inp = torch.rand(val).mul(100).long()
    with torch.no_grad():
        torch.embedding_renorm_(weights, inp, 1.0, 2)
    print("This should be None: ", weights.grad_fn)

run(1000)
run(1001)
```
Outputs:
```
Running : 1000
This should be None:  None
Running : 1001
This should be None:  <CopySlices object at 0x7f02faa5e7a8>
```

Current supposition is that multi-threaded operations and thread local NoGradGuard could be problematic.

cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @jerryzh168 @SsnL @albanD @gqchen @VitalyFedyunin @ngimel @mruberry
comments:
[albanD | 2019-10-22T20:25:25Z]
## Identification of the current problem
So the problem is that `parallel_for` does not propagate thread local states into the thread pool it uses.
The problematic states here are the `GradMode::enabled` and wether or not to unwrap variables during dispatch.
Indeed, in the original function, we work with Tensors and GradMode is disabled. While in some of the worker threads, we now work with Variables and with GradMode enabled.

But after a quick look, others could be leading to unexpected behavior as well like
- `in_parallel_region_` used to check whether we are already in a parallel region, worker threads could actually re-spawn more threads in some cases?
- many jit stuff
- cuda current streams

## Main question

Is `parallel_for` supposed to be usable with Tensors. And so running operations on Tensors in each worker thread should do the same thing?
Or is `parallel_for` supposed to work only with pointers of raw data: Tensors should be unpacked before and only pointers should be passed to it?

## Proposed answer

After discussion, the main point is that making `parallel_for` work with Tensor operations is actually a big feature (as in a lot of work).

title: torch.no_grad() context manager seems to leak memory
body:
I have a lazy loop that is used to evaluate the model. This version doesn't use any noticeable memory (memory_allocated < 1Gb):
```python
def apply_model(data_loader, model):
    for dataset_name_, audio_path_, reference_, x, xlen, y, ylen in data_loader:
        x, xlen, y, ylen = x.to(args.device), xlen.to(args.device), y.to(args.device), ylen.to(args.device)
        with torch.no_grad():
            log_probs, output_lengths, loss = map(model(x, xlen, y = y, ylen = ylen).get, ['log_probs', 'output_lengths', 'loss'])
        yield log_probs
```

The context manager version:
```python
@torch.no_grad()
def apply_model(data_loader, model):
    print('memory_allocated', torch.cuda.memory_allocated() / 1e9, 'memory_cached', torch.cuda.memory_cached() / 1e9)
    for dataset_name_, audio_path_, reference_, x, xlen, y, ylen in data_loader:

        yield log_probs
```

title: ConvTranspose2d much slower with output_padding set
body:
## 🐛 Bug

A `nn.ConvTranspose2d` can be up to two orders of magnitude slower when the `output_padding` option is set to a nonzero value then when it isn't.

## To Reproduce

```
class Test(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, output_padding):
        super().__init__()

        self.c1 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(128, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=2,
                                     padding=1, output_padding=output_padding)
        self.c2 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=2,
                                     padding=1, output_padding=output_padding)
        self.c3 = nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 3, kernel_size=3, stride=2,
                                     padding=1, output_padding=output_padding)
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.c1(x)
        x = nn.functional.relu(x)
        x = self.c2(x)
        x = nn.functional.relu(x)
        x = self.c3(x)
        x = nn.functional.relu(x)
        return x

def test(output_padding):
    network = Test(output_padding=output_padding).cuda()
    x = torch.rand((1028, 128, 6, 6)).cuda()


    for i in range(5):
        start = time.time()
        for i in range(10):
            network(x)
        print((time.time() - start) / 10)

test((0, 0))
test((1, 1))
```

On my V100 machine, I get timings of about 0.0004s per forward pass with `output_padding=(0, 0)` and about .05s with `output_padding=(1, 1)`.

## Expected behavior

Given that the `output_padding` option has minimal effect on the number of FLOPs required to compute the function, I would expect the computation time to be similar with and without the option.

title: Memory Leak & Performance Decrease on AMD CPU with PyTorch >1.3
body:
## 🐛 Bug

It seems there is a memory leak and performance decrease within torch.matmul on AMD processors and PyTorch >1.3. When I multiply two 'big' zero matrices 100000 times, the computation time is four times as long as for PyTorch >1.3 and the computation leaks around 600 MB. Interestingly, I can only observe this behaviour on AMD Processors running PyTorch greater 1.4. When running PyTorch 1.3.1 everything works fine.

For Intel Processors (OS = Ubuntu & Mac) running PyTorch 1.4.0, I did not observe the memory leak or the performance decrease.

## To Reproduce
```
import os
import numpy as np
import psutil
import torch
from tqdm import trange

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("\n\n\n")
    n_samples = 100000

    pid = os.getpid()
    prev_memoryUse = 0.0

    py = psutil.Process(pid)
    init_mem = py.memory_info()[0] / 2. ** 30
    print(f"PyTorch Version {torch.__version__}")
    for i in trange(n_samples, desc="Torch Memory:", ncols=100):
        tmp = torch.matmul(torch.zeros((1, 256, 256)), torch.zeros((1, 256, 2)))

    memoryUse = py.memory_info()[0] / 2. ** 30
    print(f"Torch Memory: Memory = {memoryUse:.3e}Gb \t Delta Memory = {memoryUse - init_mem:+.3e}Gb")
```

[mingfeima | 2020-02-17T07:41:07Z]
@hl475 I do witness performance regression for certain configuration of inputs after switching a similar CPU. On particular, the following two are most serious:
* cat_M128_N1024_K2_dim1_cpu
* cat_M512_N512_K2_dim1_cpu

The performance regression should have come from in-efficient use of L1 cache. In the **PT OP Benchmark**, the input tensor list of [cat_test.py](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/benchmarks/operator_benchmark/pt/cat_test.py#L44) is actually the same tensor, e.g. [input_one, input_one].

In the old TH implementation, when iterating the length of the input tensor list, each inner line of `input_one` will be loaded only once and cached in L1 (size here is 1024 * 2 * 4 bytes).
However in #30806, the TensorIterator will copy the input tensors one after another, thus `input_one` will be loaded multiple times.

Anyway, I will provide a patch to make a fast path for such kind of scenario.

title: torch.distributions.Categorical.sample uses unnecessary huge amount of memory
body:
## 🐛 Bug

When sampling from a torch.distributions.Categorical distribution initialized with a few distributions (e.g. 2 distributions each with 2**16 categories) the sample() functions allocates unnecessary huge amount of memory.

## To Reproduce
```
import torch
p = torch.ones([2, 2**16], device='cuda:0')
dist = torch.distributions.Categorical(p)
dist.sample([2**16])
```


Output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../lib/python3.7/site-packages/IPython/core/interactiveshell.py", line 3326, in run_code
    exec(code_obj, self.user_global_ns, self.user_ns)
  File "<ipython-input-2-c4f33ee0a190>", line 4, in <module>
    dist.sample([2**16])
  File ".../lib/python3.7/site-packages/torch/distributions/categorical.py", line 106, in sample
    probs_2d = probs.reshape(-1, self._num_events)
RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 32.00 GiB (GPU 0; 1.95 GiB total capacity; 1024.00 KiB already allocated; 1.15 GiB free; 2.00 MiB reserved in total by PyTorch)

## Expected behavior

Looking into the torch.distributions.Categorical source shows:
```
    def sample(self, sample_shape=torch.Size()):
        sample_shape = self._extended_shape(sample_shape)
        param_shape = sample_shape + torch.Size((self._num_events,))
        probs = self.probs.expand(param_shape)
        probs_2d = probs.reshape(-1, self._num_events)
        sample_2d = torch.multinomial(probs_2d, 1, True)
        return sample_2d.reshape(sample_shape)
```
The last three lines allocate the new memory and use it. probs_2d becomes a potentially huge tensor with repeated information.
The following code snippet solves it and uses much less memory, but I'm not sure it covers all cases and whether the order of the dimensions is as expected. It's not thoroughly tested.
```
    def sample(self, sample_shape=torch.Size()):
        if not isinstance(sample_shape, torch.Size):
            sample_shape = torch.Size(sample_shape)
        samples = torch.multinomial(self.probs, sample_shape.numel(), True)
        return samples.reshape([-1] + list(sample_shape))
```

@jjabo - I think one issue is that the `probs` argument to `Categorical` can be batched (n-dimensional where n > 2, the last dim is taken as the event dim), whereas the argument to `multinomial` has to be 1 or 2D. I think the issue with the current code is the `expand` step which in this case expands probs to have shape more than `2**16 x 2**16`! I think we should be able to use your solution to work for the batched case too as follows:

```python
    def sample(self, sample_shape=torch.Size()):
        probs_2d = self.probs.reshape(-1, self._num_events)
        samples_2d = torch.multinomial(probs_2d, sample_shape.numel(), True).T
        return samples_2d.reshape(self._extended_shape(sample_shape))
```

title: Gradient update of a sparse matrix results in a memory leak
body:
## 🐛 Bug

Gradient update with `parameter.add_(val, grad)` of sparse matrices results in a memory leak that is not present in dense matrices with the same computation.

Freeing cache/calling the garbage collector does not remove the problem. The result of the computation is the same for both the sparse and the dense networks. The backward pass without an update of the matrix does not cause this problem.

## To Reproduce

Take a network that computes `||Wx||_F^2` with either a dense or a sparse `W` and minimize it. The part that produces the bug is
```
with torch.no_grad():
    net.weights.add_(-lr, net.weights.grad)
```
(Updating `net.weights.data` without in-place operations results in the same behaviour)

#### Steps to reproduce the behavior:
Imports and printing functions. The script prints the currently allocated tensors and the memory stats **after** zeroing the gradient.
```
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import gc

def print_stats(i):
    print('\nIteration %d' % i)
    print('Resources:')
    for obj in gc.get_objects():  # as in https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/how-to-debug-causes-of-gpu-memory-leaks/6741/2
        try:
            if torch.is_tensor(obj) or (hasattr(obj, 'data') and torch.is_tensor(obj.data)):
                print('\t', type(obj), obj.size())
        except:
            pass

    print('\t{0: <15}\t{1: >6} MB'.format('Allocated', torch.cuda.memory_allocated(device) // 1024 ** 2))
    print('\t{0: <15}\t{1: >6} MB'.format('Max allocated', torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated(device) // 1024 ** 2))
    print('\t{0: <15}\t{1: >6} MB'.format('Cached', torch.cuda.memory_cached(device) // 1024 ** 2))
    print('\t{0: <15}\t{1: >6} MB'.format('Max cached', torch.cuda.max_memory_cached(device) // 1024 ** 2))
```
The sparse and the dense networks are the same, but the first one uses a sparse `W` and `torch.sparse.mm(W,x)` instead of dense `W`/`torch.mm(W,x)` (`W` is `1 x n`):
```
def make_sparse_weights(input_length):
    values = torch.ones(input_length, dtype=torch.float)
    indices = torch.tensor([[0, i] for i in range(input_length)], dtype=torch.long).t()
    return torch.sparse.FloatTensor(indices, values, size=(1, input_length))


class SparseNetwork(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_length):
        super().__init__()
        self.weights = nn.Parameter(make_sparse_weights(input_length),
                                    requires_grad=True)

    def forward(self, x):
        return torch.norm(torch.sparse.mm(self.weights, x)) ** 2


class DenseNetwork(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_length):
        super().__init__()
        self.weights = nn.Parameter(make_sparse_weights(input_length).to_dense(),
                                    requires_grad=True)

    def forward(self, x):
        return torch.norm(torch.mm(self.weights, x)) ** 2
```
The script does plain SGD with an option to free cache/collect garbage after zeroing the gradient:
```
def run_net(net, x, lr, device, n_iterations,
            update_weight=True, empty_cache=False, collect_garbage=False):
    for i in range(n_iterations):
        # free the gradients and print resources

        if net.weights.grad is not None:
            net.weights.grad.detach_()
            net.weights.grad.zero_()

        if empty_cache:
            torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        if collect_garbage:
            gc.collect()

        if i % 1000 == 0:
            print_stats(i)

        # compute
        loss = net(x)
        loss.backward()

        # update
        if update_weight and net.weights.grad is not None:
            # the SGD implementation with p.data.add_()
            # throws an error and suggests this solution:

            with torch.no_grad():
                net.weights.add_(-lr, net.weights.grad)

        if i % 1000 == 0:
            print('Loss: %f' % loss.item())
```

title: Memory Leak in autograd using ndarray[None]
body:
Here is an example of what seems to be a memory leak in pytorch, although it could be numpy?

```
import numpy as np
import gc
import resource
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.autograd import Variable

model = nn.Linear(100, 2)

i = 0
while True:
    i += 1

    np_arr = np.ones(100).astype(np.float32)
    tensor = torch.from_numpy(np_arr[None]) # Issue seems to be use of [None] or [np.newaxis]
    variable = Variable(tensor)
    output = model(variable)

    if i % 1000 == 0:
        gc.collect()
        max_mem_used = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
        print("{:.2f} MB".format(max_mem_used / 1024))
```

The leak was only occurring when using the `[None]` or `[np.newaxis]` array unsqueezing methods in numpy. Also worth noting that the issue is resolved by removing the `.astype(np.float32)` from `np_arr` and casting the torch tensor to `float()` type.

An easy workaround is to reshape the array after turning it into a torch Tensor.

title: Curreent SyncBatchNorm (a synchronized implementation) slow down DDP training
body:
## 🚀 Feature
<!-- A clear and concise description of the feature proposal -->
An asynchronized implementation w.r.t to the host thread

## Motivation

<!-- Please outline the motivation for the proposal. Is your feature request related to a problem? e.g., I'm always frustrated when [...]. If this is related to another GitHub issue, please link here too -->

Current implementation of ``SyncBatchNorm`` is not only synchronized with other workers but also block the host thread, so the host cannot continue issue computing task to the GPU like it does with ``Module`` without ``SyncBatchNorm``. So the GPU cannot be saturated during training.

After I do some research on the current implementation, I find there are 2 draw backs:
1. ``AllGather`` must be Synchronized with host thread to guarantee the all data is gathered. This is the main reason that host thread must be blocked in current implementation. Code is at [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/nn/modules/_functions.py#L33-L35)

2. The last argument of  ``batch_norm_gather_stats_with_counts``, a.k.a. ``counts`` must be a ``IntArrayRef``, but later is converted back into ``CUDATensor`` in [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Normalization.cu#L136-L137), which cause unnecessary ``MemcpyDtoH`` and ``MemcpyHtoD`` and also block the host thread.

Here are timelines of NVVP of DPP training with and without ``SyncBatchNorm``.
![with_sync_bn](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2868493/79064328-91db3b00-7cda-11ea-952d-4940ed80dab7.png)
![without_sync_bn](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2868493/79064331-956ec200-7cda-11ea-9076-78ea3e47b829.png)
With ``SyncBatchNorm``, forward pass is abount 700ms
Without ``SyncBatchNorm``, forward pass is about 100ms

## Pitch

<!-- A clear and concise description of what you want to happen. -->
1. NCCL colloective functions may be submit to task sequence of a stream just like other CUDA operation, so host thread does not have to be blocked in SyncBatchNorm and other synchronization operation like gradient reduction.
2.  The last argument of  ``batch_norm_gather_stats_with_counts``, a.k.a. ``counts`` should accept ``CUDATensor`` rather than ``IntArrayRef`` or list of ``int`` at Python layer.

## Alternatives

<!-- A clear and concise description of any alternative solutions or features you've considered, if any. -->

## Additional context

<!-- Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here. -->

After some further research, I found that

> ``AllGather`` must be Synchronized with host thread to guarantee the all data is gathered. This is the main reason that host thread must be blocked in current implementation. Code is at [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/nn/modules/_functions.py#L33-L35)

is not true according to [this](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/lib/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCL.hpp#L48-L50

title: Multinomial sampling without replacements is slow
body:
## 🚀 Feature
Add a faster implementation of multinomial sampling.

## Motivation
As for now, sampling without replacements is very slow because the code runs in `O(n*m)` and is sequential: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c9a1fc2b31ded472c63b227ad24859bc14131f42/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/MultinomialKernel.cpp#L105-L127.

## Pitch

There exists a faster way to sample from multinomial distribution without replacements: https://stackoverflow.com/a/20548895/1894478

python code is pretty simple:
```python
def WeightedSelectionWithoutReplacement(weights, m):
    elt = [(math.log(random.random()) / weights[i], i) for i in range(len(weights))]
    return [x[1] for x in heapq.nlargest(m, elt)]
```
which runs in `O(n+mlogm)` with possible parallelization to `O(n)` part.

title: gpu_tensor.to("cpu", non_blocking=True) is blocking
body:
## 🐛 Bug

```
>>> a = torch.tensor(100000, device="cuda")
>>> b = a.to("cpu", non_blocking=True)
>>> b.is_pinned()
False
```

The cpu dst memory is created as pageable, so the memcpy is host blocking (["For transfers from device memory to pageable host memory, the function will return only once the copy has completed."](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-runtime-api/api-sync-behavior.html#api-sync-behavior)).  We have one user with evidence that the pageable memcpy also blocks side streams (ie DALI dataloader streams).

Fix might be as simple as setting [options.pinned_memory](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/c767d65cafc2615bcee9ec1bbc8d5dadc07ea0e8/c10/core/TensorOptions.h#L216) for the new dst tensor around [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/1f7557d173c8e9066ed9542ada8f4a09314a7e17/aten/src/ATen/native/TensorConversions.cpp#L24) in to_impl.  I'd PR it myself but if it turns out to be a rabbit hole (for example, since pinned cpu memory is a valuable resource, do we want the returned tensor to live in pinned cpu memory by default, or do we want `to` to include a further host-side memcopy or unpinning such that the returned tensor lives in pageable memory?) I can't afford to go down another rabbit hole right this second.  Filing now so we don't forget.

body:
## 🐛 Bug

After some quantization operations are called on cuda tensors (in particular, _make_per_tensor_quantized_tensor, maybe some others) all subsequent cpu allocations are using pinned memory
## To Reproduce
```
import torch
x = torch.randn(3)
print(x.is_pinned()) # False, as expected
q_int = torch.randint(0, 100, [1, 2, 3], device="cuda", dtype=torch.int)

print(x.is_pinned()) #True, all host allocations after this point are in pinned memory

Quantization operations should not affect subsequent cpu allocations
This is important because with pinned allocations all the cpu operations will be slowed down significantly. E.g. `test_histogram_observer` runs for 40s in isolation, but for 400s if there were previous cuda quantization operations, and all the allocations as a result are forced to be pinned allocations.

title: Use undefined as Tensor of zeroes in the python Function API
body:
We now fully support undefined Tensors in the backward pass to represent a Tensor full of zeroes.
We should leverage this and stop creating full size Tensors for custom Function (both on python and cpp side)

cc @ezyang @SsnL @albanD @zou3519 @gqchen @yf225 @glaringlee @VitalyFedyunin @ngimel
comments:
[albanD | 2020-07-14T20:15:31Z]
More details of the two part that are covered by this issue.

1. Stop materializing outputs
For this part, we just want to make sure that `None` or `undefined` Tensors returned by the custom backward are passed as `undefined` to the rest of the computations.
The only BC breaking change this leads to is when this output is directly linked to either an `AccumulateGrad` (and so the .grad field of a leaf Tensor) or an input Tensor from `autograd.grad()`. In this case, the user will get None/undefined for Tensors that used to get a Tensor full of 0s.
This is properly handled by our optimizers and will cause clear errors for users that expect a Tensor here.
We already use None, an error or a Tensor full of 0s to represent a Tensor full of 0s and which one the user get depends on the internal implementation.

2. Stop materializing the inputs (can be done in a second PR)
This one would mean that we stop creating Tensor full of 0s and give undefined Tensor in cpp and None in python.
This one is more problematic from a BC point of view because it means that all the user's custom Function need to handle such special inputs.
Given that this is only for performance in very specific case, we can add this as an opt-in feature. So the behavior wouldn't change for current users but users that define a static attribute `dont_materialize_grads = True` will get the new behavior and get None/undefined gradients that they need to properly handle.

---

[ssnl | 2020-07-15T01:27:44Z]
> This is properly handled by our optimizers and will cause clear errors for users that expect a Tensor here.
We already use None, an error or a Tensor full of 0s to represent a Tensor full of 0s and which one the user get depends on the internal implementation.

I just want to say that this is **not** properly handled by the optimizers. For the ones doing weight decay and/or momentum, having `None` gradient vs having `zero` gradient do different things. It is use to decide when a variable starts to accept momentum / weight decay. I would agree with the argument that this is a somewhat weird behavior though.

---

[albanD | 2020-07-15T13:59:23Z]
> I just want to say that this is not properly handled by the optimizers.

Good point. It is handled but not the exact same way.

My reasoning is:
- We don't guarantee this behavior (you can get None, an error or a Tensor full of 0s already). So the behavior for inputs independent of the output is already in a bad state.
- This will affect a very small number of users
- A user returning None from their backward will get None for their .grad field which feels consistent
- The performance improvement can be significant depending on the tasks (following Node will also skip computations)
- Drawback: Some user custom Functions that are independent of the input (from the grad point of view, not forward point of view) will now return None gradient instead of a Tensor full of 0s.
  - This can confuse the user for that used to get a Tensor full of 0s. But I would argue that None is more consistent if their custom function returned None.
  - This will change the optimizer behavior.

Do you agree that this BC-breaking change is worth it?

@albanD It would break some reproducibility silently though, which is my main concern. I think we should more properly define what to do with momentum/decay when grad is `None` and zeros. Also another thing to think about is whether we want to change `.zero_grad()` to set `None` instead.

Yes we marked it as BC-breaking.

title: Poor performance of dynamic quantazation
body:
## 🐛 Bug

I am experimenting with dynamic quantization as described here:
https://pytorch.org/blog/introduction-to-quantization-on-pytorch/

I got a pretty good speedup when running with a single thread. (This is a GRPC server application that serves pytorch models). However, I do not see any improvement when using multiple threads and processing multiple concurrent requests. This does not happen when dynamic quantization is not being used: I see pretty good scaling up to about 10 threads. The CPU utilization when running with 10 threads but without quantization is well over 700%. However, when dynamic quantization is enabled, CPU load peaks around 150%, meaning that most of the cores sit idle.

This leads me to believe that python's GIL is the culprit. I noticed that in many parts of the code, pytorch does the following:

pybind11::gil_scoped_release no_gil;

But this does not happen in qlinear_dynamic.cpp which runs on dynamic quantization. This again implies that when dynamic quantization is used, GIL does not get released. This would certainly explain why we see improved performance with one thread but not with multiple threads.

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 environment variable.

2. Load any model and apply dynamic quantization:

model = torch.quantization.quantize_dynamic(model, {torch.nn.Linear}, dtype=torch.qint8)

3. Use threadpool to make multiple concurrent calls to to the model.

## 🐛 Bug

There seems to be a significant performance drop after migrating the istft from torchaudio to pytorch.
migration discussed here [#34827](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/34827)
I've also noticed the performance gap increases with greater n_fft.

import torch

n_fft = 2**15
x = torch.rand(size=[1, n_fft//2 + 1, 10, 2])
start = time.time()
y = torch.functional.istft(x,n_fft)
end = time.time()
print(end - start)
```

title: torch.inverse() performing very poorly on GPU vs CPU
body:
## 🐛 Bug
We observed a big increase in inference latency after adding `torch.inverse()` in the code path. After investigation and comparison with moving the op to CPU we found that there is a huge difference in performance of that op on GPU vs CPU.
The matrix size in our case is 4x4 which small for the GPU but `torch.inverse()` should be using `magma` library which has heuristics to move the op to CPU. We didn't see any magma invocations as well.

Based on @ptrblck suggestion we tried `inverse` on batched matrix to see if that made any difference but that also didn't result in any improvement.

**Performance Difference:**
```
╰─ python torch_inverse_exp.py
GPU Time: 8.78560 ms
CPU Time: 0.07149 ms
cpu/gpu: 122.90x
```
We increased the matrix dimensions to 1024x1024 but even then GPU is slower than CPU:
```
╰─ python torch_inverse_exp.py
GPU Time: 17.25289 ms
CPU Time: 9.54982 ms
cpu/gpu: 1.81x
```
## To Reproduce
Here is the snippet of code which can be run to reproduce the performance difference:
```
import torch
import time

a = torch.randn(4,4).cuda()
torch.cuda.synchronize()

num_iter = 100
def test1():
    s = time.time()
    for i in range(num_iter):
        x = torch.inverse(a)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    e = time.time()
    gpu_time = ((e - s)/num_iter)
    return  gpu_time

def test2():
    s = time.time()
    for i in range(num_iter):
        b = a.to('cpu')
        d = torch.inverse(b)
        y = d.to('cuda')
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    e = time.time()
    cpu_time = ((e - s)/num_iter)
    return  cpu_time

gpu_time = test1()
print("GPU Time: {:.5f} ms".format(gpu_time*1000))

cpu_time = test2()
print("CPU Time: {:.5f} ms".format( cpu_time*1000))

print("cpu/gpu: {:.2f}x ".format(gpu_time/cpu_time))

title: linear function and the different convs functions retain unnecessary buffers
body:
## 🐛 Bug

The function `torch.nn.functional` but also the different `torch.nn.functional.convXd` keep allocated the input also when the weight does not require the gradient.

## To Reproduce

The following code shows the issue by comparing `torch.nn.functional` against a custom implementation of it.

```
import torch

from torch.nn.functional import linear


# Creating the customized function
class MyLinear(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, i, w):

        if ctx.needs_input_grad[1]:
            ctx.save_for_backward(w, i)
        else:
            ctx.save_for_backward(w)
        return i.mm(w.t())

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_output):
        saved = ctx.saved_tensors
        return grad_output.mm(saved[0]), grad_output.t().mm(saved[1]) if ctx.needs_input_grad[1] else None

# Input requiring gradient
x = torch.rand(1000, 10).cuda().requires_grad_()

# Weights NOT requiring gradient
weight = torch.rand(20, 10).cuda()


# This function performs some operations using the function f and keeps track of the
# allocated gpu memory within the function.
def test(f, x, weight):
    s = torch.cuda.memory_allocated()
    x = x + 2
    x = f(x, weight)
    print(f"Allocated memory: {torch.cuda.memory_allocated() - s}")
    return x


# I report the amount of allocated memory by torch.nn.functional
print("Test Pytorch linear")
y1 = test(linear, x, weight)

# I report the amount of allocated memory by the customized implementation
print("\nTest MyLinear")
y2 = test(MyLinear.apply, x, weight)

# Check that the obtained outputs agree
print(f"\nSame output? {y1.allclose(y2)}")

y1.norm().backward()
z1 = x.grad.clone()

x.grad.zero_()
y2.norm().backward()
z2 = x.grad.clone()

# Check that the gradient wrt input agrees.
print(f"Same gradient? {z1.allclose(z2)}")
```

The output I get:
```
Test Pytorch linear
Allocated memory: 120832

Test MyLinear
Allocated memory: 80384

Same output? True
Same gradient? True
```


## Expected behavior

`torch.nn.autograd.linear` should return the same amount of memory allocated by the custom implementation.
Specifically, when the weight does not require the gradient, the input should not be stored for later use.

NOTE: this applies not just to `linear` but also to the convolution operator of Pytorch.

title: Improvement of autograd engine original task placement in worker threads
body:
Currently, when a call to the autograd engine is done, the original task is always placed on the CPU worker queue.
While this works great, it can lead to surprising behavior, in particular when re-entrant autograd happen from a GPU thread.

Indeed, even though the whole code runs on a GPU and should run serially on the GPU thread, the original task happening on the CPU can lead to non-determinism and bad ordering of the execution (which can lead to very bad memory usage when using checkpointing and independent branches).

From the top of my head, I think we should:
- Remove [this code](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/4fc525e72976a470ca7a56264734c3cb0afe1fe8/torch/csrc/autograd/engine.cpp#L867) when there is a single input: we can just use that input's grad_fn as the graph root. That will be better perf-wise, especially for very small graphs.
- Change [this code](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/4fc525e72976a470ca7a56264734c3cb0afe1fe8/torch/csrc/autograd/engine.cpp#L892-L893) to push on the right queue based on the inputs (mimicking the logic [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/4fc525e72976a470ca7a56264734c3cb0afe1fe8/torch/csrc/autograd/input_buffer.cpp#L121-L137)).

Even though I wouldn't expect anyone to rely on this, this would be BC-breaking. But I think the determinism and gain in memory in these cases will be worth it.

cc @ezyang @albanD @zou3519 @gqchen @pearu @nikitaved @gchanan @SsnL
comments:
[wanchaol | 2020-08-12T18:54:22Z]
Seems to me that the main change here is to determine the correct device ready queue for GraphRoot by examing the inputs device? This sounds good to me as I didn't see any potential issues for this approach.

For distributed engine, we are still doing similar thing like the current local autograd engine, but it's a bit different, we maintain a `ready_queue` per GraphRoot, and always push to this newly allocated ready queue (see code [here](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/54c05fa34e1fbbb5096746a8ae92e27a08116de4/torch/csrc/distributed/autograd/engine/dist_engine.cpp#L291)). since it's manually polled off tasks from this newly allocated queue, the approach you proposed might not just work for the dist engine. @pritamdamania to confirm here.

---

[albanD | 2020-08-12T19:05:30Z]
> we maintain a ready_queue per GraphRoot

What about the re-entrant case?
A particular example that can be problematic is something like
```python
inp = torch.rand(10, requires_grad=True, device="cuda")
out1 = checkpoint(f1, inp)
out2 = checkpoint(f2, inp)
loss = crit(out1, out2)
loss.backward()
```
Here, when the first checkpoint backward is hit, the re-entrant enqueues the GraphRoot on the CPU queue. And so the GPU worker starts doing the second checkpoint (recomputing another forward, etc).
So there will be no memory benefit by using checkpoint in this case because the engine runs both of them in an interleaved manner even even though they only contain GPU tasks that should run sequentially on a single thread.

What would happen if we do this in the distributed engine?

---

[wanchaol | 2020-08-14T00:10:01Z]
> What about the re-entrant case?
> A particular example that can be problematic is something like
>
> ```python
> inp = torch.rand(10, requires_grad=True, device="cuda")
> out1 = checkpoint(f1, inp)
> out2 = checkpoint(f2, inp)
> loss = crit(out1, out2)
> loss.backward()
> ```
>
> Here, when the first checkpoint backward is hit, the re-entrant enqueues the GraphRoot on the CPU queue. And so the GPU worker starts doing the second checkpoint (recomputing another forward, etc).
> So there will be no memory benefit by using checkpoint in this case because the engine runs both of them in an interleaved manner even even though they only contain GPU tasks that should run sequentially on a single thread.
>
> What would happen if we do this in the distributed engine?

I think when we added the functionality of maintaining separate ready_queues for each graph root, we had the assumption that we don't support re-entrant bnackward case in dist_engine. And there's no distinction for all ready_queues in the dist_engine as we all do this `execute until empty` style on a separate CPU thread (no dedicated GPU thread).

For the case that you mentioned above, I agree with you that it's kinda losing the benefits of checkpointing. I don't really know how would checkpointing works together with the dist engine in today's design. @pritamdamania can you chime in here?

---

[pritamdamania87 | 2020-08-18T23:36:17Z]
reentrant-backward/checkpointing are not officially supported in the distributed engine and we explicitly didn't target support for this to keep the original implementation simple.

Although to resolve this issue for the distributed engine, why can't we first check the root to see if it needs to be enqueued on the GPU queue and push it to the appropriate GPU queue instead of enqueueing it on the CPU queue. If we have a CPU task, we create a new queue and just execute until empty.

---

[albanD | 2020-11-10T21:01:48Z]
After more exploration, the change in the threading system, when we perform re-entrant from a GPU worker thread, it is (wrongfully?) picking up the GPU worker thread queue as its new CPU queue and so the new task is actually enqueued on the right queue.
So the non-determinism mentioned above does not actually exist in master anymore and this won't be BC-breaking.

title: PyTorch binaries for macOS has serial at::parallel_for because it is built with OpenMP which  is not available
body:
A silly performance test linearly depends(1000 times slower on 1000x larger tenor) on tensor size on macOS(with 6 cores i9) but  can be 4-10 time faster on Linux or Windows:
```
In [2]: t = torch.ones(1000, device='cpu')

In [3]: timeit t.pow(123)
7.45 µs ± 343 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100000 loops each)

In [4]: t = torch.ones(1000000, device='cpu')

In [5]: timeit t.pow(123)
5.83 ms ± 246 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)
```

`torch.__config__.parallel_info()` says for all OSes that PyTorch was compiled with OpenMP but it's not actually available on macOS:

```
at::get_num_threads() : 1
at::get_num_interop_threads() : 6
OpenMP not found
...
ATen parallel backend: OpenMP
```

Version.cpp:
```
std::string get_openmp_version() {
#ifdef _OPENMP
...
#else
  ss << "OpenMP not found";
#endif
}
```

ParallelOpenMP.h:
```
inline void parallel_for(..., const F& f) {
...
#ifdef _OPENMP
...
#else
  f(begin, end);
#endif
}
```
which looks like serial invocation.

This affects at least PyTorch 1.3.0-1.6.0 both pip and conda
